cards.b:
Rivers, groundwater and noise are classic GS-III topics. Prelims tests terms like BOD and COD. Mains asks for causes, laws and schemes like Namami Gange.

One idea ties everything: pollution is not only about industry. Sewage and farming matter most in India.

Dissolved oxygen (DO) must be high for aquatic life. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) shows organic pollution: high BOD means low DO. COD (chemical oxygen demand) includes chemically oxidisable matter and is higher than BOD.

Eutrophication from nutrients causes algal bloom and fish kills. India’s biggest source is untreated sewage.

CPCB's criteria for bathing water ask for DO of 5 mg/l or more and BOD of 3 mg/l or less. Other indicators are the faecal coliform count, which shows sewage contamination, plus pH, turbidity and total dissolved solids. Bioindicators help too: some insect larvae such as stoneflies live only in clean water, while sludge worms survive in polluted water.

Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis (Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh). Arsenic above 0.01 mg/L causes skin and cancer problems (Ganga plains, West Bengal, Bihar). Nitrate rises from fertiliser. Over-extraction also draws up salt and uranium in some areas.

The Central Ground Water Board monitors this.

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 set up the CPCB and State Boards. The Water Cess Act 1977 taxes water use. Jan Vishwas amendments (2023–24) replaced many jail terms with penalties.

The Ganga Action Plan began in 1985. Namami Gange (2014) is run by the National Mission for Clean Ganga with sewage treatment as its core. The Ganga became a National River in 2008. Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) aims at tap water in every rural home.

Under the 1974 Act, no one may discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream without the State Board's consent. It was India's first modern pollution law. Under the Environment Protection Act 1986 the Centre sets effluent standards. Practical tools are sewage treatment plants (STPs), common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) and zero liquid discharge norms. Namami Gange also covers industrial effluent monitoring and riverfront development.

Causes: excess pesticide and fertiliser, industrial effluent, mining, solid waste, irrigation with polluted water. Result: salinity, alkalinity, loss of microbes, heavy metals entering food.

The Soil Health Card scheme (2015) promotes balanced use. Organic farming schemes such as PKVY reduce chemical load. Contaminated site rules remain weak in India.

Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 under the EPA give day (6 am to 10 pm) and night limits.

Day/night limits in dB(A): industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence zone 50/40. Silence zones extend to 100 m around hospitals, schools and courts. Loudspeakers are restricted between 10 pm and 6 am with limited exceptions.

Thermal pollution comes from power plant coolant water. It lowers oxygen in rivers. Oil spills harm seabirds and coasts. The MARPOL convention (1973/78) regulates ship pollution.

Plastic and microplastics now reach even the Himalaya and the deep sea.

cards.h: Law is strong, enforcement is weak
cards.b:
State Pollution Control Boards are short of staff and funds, and sometimes politically pressured. Decriminalisation (Jan Vishwas) is defended as ease of doing business but criticised as weakening deterrence.

The polluter pays principle is accepted, yet recovery of environmental compensation is slow. River cleaning has focused on building plants; poor running and no ecological flow remain problems.

NGT orders and court-imposed environmental compensation have forced some cleanups, yet many orders go unmet. Audits have pointed to unspent funds and delays in river projects. Experts propose independent monitoring, real-time online emission monitoring, a larger role for communities, and treating wastewater as a resource for reuse in industry and farming.

The Yamuna in Delhi, the Ganga near Kanpur and the Adyar and Cooum in Chennai are standard examples. The NGT has monitored Ganga and Yamuna cleaning.

The Supreme Court’s M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Ganga tanneries) and the Vellore Citizens case (1996) established the precautionary principle and polluter pays.

Mains-style: “Despite crores spent, Indian rivers remain polluted. Why? Suggest reforms.” Structure: causes (sewage gap, industry, agriculture); programmes (GAP, Namami Gange); failures (design, running costs, ecological flow, governance); way forward (decentralised treatment, reuse, river basin authorities).

Prelims tip: BOD high means worse water. Fluoride limit 1.5 mg/L. Silence zone 100 m. Water Act 1974.
